titleEn: Nigerian Pidgin is the one language almost every Nigerian shares
facts: Naijá, as scholars call it, began in the 17th and 18th centuries from contact between British traders and coastal African communities, and it is now the speech form with the widest geographical coverage in Nigeria.
It has its own pronouns, tense particles and idioms, and linguists treat it as an English-based creole rather than as badly spoken English.
Because it belongs to no single ethnic group, it works as a neutral code in markets, on radio, in football commentary and between strangers from different regions.
Vocabulary and intonation shift between Lagos, Port Harcourt and Kano Pidgin, drawing on Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa respectively.
Since the 2010s it has appeared in advertising, literature and some broadcasting, though official documents stay in Standard English.
exampleEn: Two strangers from different states meet at a Lagos bus stop; neither switches to the other's first language, both slide into Pidgin, and the conversation proceeds without anyone having to claim an identity.
qualificationEn: Naijá is not one uniform variety, written Pidgin is still unsettled, and many Nigerians switch to Standard English in formal or unfamiliar settings.

expression.glossEn: How are you? — the everyday greeting in Nigeria's widest shared second language

region: Sahel — northern Nigeria and southern Niger
titleEn: Hausa: the Sahel's market language, written in Arabic letters
facts: Hausa is spoken by more than 90 million people and serves as a lingua franca across northern Nigeria, southern Niger, northern Cameroon, Ghana, Benin, Chad and parts of Sudan.
Caravan trade made it the practical language of Sahelian markets long before colonial borders, and it remains the default language of bargaining in Kano and Zinder.
Ajami is the adaptation of the Arabic script to write Hausa and other West African languages, with a long history of poetry, medicine and correspondence.
Colonial schooling promoted the Latin-based boko script, and Ajami retreated from formal use while surviving in Qur'anic education, talismans and women's poetry.
Hausa radio drama, BBC and Deutsche Welle broadcasts helped standardise a Kano-based variety that is understood far beyond the city.
exampleEn: A trader in Kano writes a receipt in Ajami for a customer who reads Arabic script more comfortably than Latin letters, then repeats the price in spoken Hausa.
qualificationEn: Hausa is not one variety — Kano, Sokoto and Zaria speech differ — and Ajami literacy is far from universal among Hausa speakers.

expression.glossEn: Good morning — literally 'how did you sleep?', the standard morning greeting

titleEn: Sheng: Nairobi's youth language that keeps outgrowing itself
facts: Sheng began among Nairobi's urban youth as a cant mixing Swahili grammar with English words and borrowings from Kikuyu, Luo, Luhya and other Kenyan languages.
It is tied to matatu culture, music and school playgrounds, and its vocabulary turns over fast enough that older speakers often cannot follow current slang.
It has spread beyond Nairobi to other Kenyan towns and into Tanzania and Uganda, and it now appears in political campaigns, radio and advertising.
Because it is not tied to one ethnic group, it lets young people signal urban identity rather than ethnic origin.
Teachers and examiners have long argued about Sheng in schools; it is rarely written in official contexts but thrives in text messages, social media and song lyrics.
exampleEn: Two students from different home languages meet at a Nairobi matatu stage, settle into Sheng within a sentence, then switch back to English when the lecture starts.
qualificationEn: Sheng is not a single stable variety; its vocabulary is local and short-lived, and many Kenyans use it only in informal, age-specific settings.

expression.glossEn: How's it going? — a greeting that signals you are part of the same urban register

titleEn: N'Ko: a script invented in 1949 to write Manding without French
facts: Solomana Kanté devised N'Ko in 1949 in Kankan, Guinea, as a writing system for the Manding languages spoken across Guinea, Mali, Côte d'Ivoire and neighbouring countries.
The name means 'I say' in Manding, and the script runs right to left, partly echoing Arabic, though its letter shapes are original.
N'Ko became a vehicle of literacy and identity: it is taught in private schools and Qur'anic schools, used for religious and medical texts, and has its own newspapers and digital fonts.
Kanté's movement treated literacy in one's own language as a form of independence from French, and N'Ko classes spread through Manding-speaking communities from the 1950s.
Computer and phone support added in the 2000s made N'Ko usable on social media and in publishing.
exampleEn: A bookseller in Bamako sells a N'Ko alphabet primer next to a N'Ko translation of a medical pamphlet, and a customer reads both without switching to French.
qualificationEn: N'Ko is not the only script for Manding — Latin-based orthographies remain standard in state schools — and N'Ko literacy is uneven across the region.

expression.glossEn: N'Ko — literally 'I say' in the Manding languages, and the name of the script itself

titleEn: Tsotsitaal and Camtho: the township registers that hide and reveal
facts: Tsotsitaal grew in Johannesburg's townships from mixed Afrikaans, Zulu, Sotho, Tswana and English; the word joins 'tsotsi' (thug) with Afrikaans 'taal' (language).
It is a register rather than a mother tongue: speakers switch into it to mark style, toughness or solidarity, then return to their home language.
Camtho (iscamtho) is the newer, more Zulu- and Sotho-based register of the same townships, and it changes quickly to keep outsiders guessing.
The registers carry vocabulary for money, police, prison and status, and they have fed South African music, film and advertising.
Because they encode local identity, they are performed self-consciously: young men use them, parents complain about them, and researchers study them as urban language change.
exampleEn: In a Soweto taxi rank two young men greet in Camtho, switch to Zulu to include an older woman, then return to Camtho once she has gone.
qualificationEn: Tsotsitaal and Camtho are not fixed codes; their vocabularies differ by township and generation, and the two names overlap in everyday use.

expression.glossEn: thug or gangster — the word that gave Tsotsitaal its name

titleEn: Lingala, the river language that became two capitals' lingua franca
facts: Lingala is a Bantu language spoken in north-western DR Congo and the northern half of the Republic of the Congo, including both Kinshasa and Brazzaville.
It grew as a trade language along the Congo River in the late 19th century and was later used by the colonial army and administration, which pushed it far beyond its original speakers.
It has roughly 20 million native speakers and another 20 million second-language speakers, and it is the main language of Congolese popular music.
Lingala is written in the Latin alphabet with a standard orthography, but most daily use is spoken, sung and broadcast.
Kinshasa street Lingala mixes French and slang and changes with each generation, so the language of a 1960s rumba sounds different from that of a 2020s song.
exampleEn: A market trader in Kinshasa opens in Lingala, gives prices in French numbers, and switches to Swahili for a customer from the east of the country.
qualificationEn: Lingala is not the language of all Congolese — Swahili, Tshiluba and Kikongo dominate other regions — and the four national languages carry different status.

expression.glossEn: Hello — the everyday greeting across Kinshasa and Brazzaville

titleEn: Swahili: the coast's language that became East Africa's common tongue
facts: Swahili is a Bantu language that grew along the East African coast, with heavy Arabic borrowing from Indian Ocean trade and the spread of Islam.
It is an official or national language in Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda, and it is used in DR Congo, Rwanda, Burundi, Mozambique and the Comoros.
Estimates of its speakers range from about 40 million to 200 million, most of whom use it as a second language rather than a mother tongue.
Standard Swahili was codified in the 1930s around the Zanzibar dialect Kiunguja, and it became the language of schools, parliaments and the East African Community.
Tanzania's ujamaa era and universal primary education made Swahili unusually dominant there, while Kenya has kept English for much official business.
exampleEn: A bus conductor in Dar es Salaam calls the stops in Swahili, repeats the fare in English for a visitor, then jokes with the regulars in Swahili again.
qualificationEn: Official status does not mean everyone speaks Swahili at home; rural Tanzania and Kenya have many first languages, and Congolese Swahili differs sharply from the coastal standard.

expression.glossEn: How are you? — literally 'your news?', the standard greeting

titleEn: Krio, the Sierra Leonean creole that unites a multilingual state
facts: Krio is an English-based creole that developed among freed slaves and their descendants in Freetown from the late 18th century.
About 96 percent of Sierra Leone's population speaks it, mostly as a second language, and it links Temne, Mende, Limba and other groups in trade and daily interaction.
Krio has its own grammar, particles and proverbs, and its vocabulary includes English, Yoruba, Portuguese and French-derived words.
It is the main language of Freetown and of mass media, and it has a body of written literature, drama and Bible translation.
Krio coexists with the Krio ethnic identity of Freetown Creoles, although most of its speakers are not ethnically Krio.
exampleEn: A Mende farmer and a Temne trader settle a price in Krio at a Freetown market, then return to their own languages with relatives.
qualificationEn: Krio is not the same as Standard English and is not universally written; formal education and government business still rely heavily on English.

expression.glossEn: Hello — the everyday greeting in Freetown

region: Central African Republic and the Ubangi basin
titleEn: Sango: a river creole that became a national language
facts: Sango is an Ngbandi-based creole spoken mainly in the Central African Republic, with speakers also in southern Chad and DR Congo.
It is an official language of the Central African Republic and the country's main lingua franca; almost all of its roughly 5.5 million people speak it.
It began as a trade language on the Ubangi River and was standardised and promoted after independence as a language of schools and radio.
Sango has a Latin orthography, a written literature and a central place in CAR music, including the pioneering work of musician Antoine Doko.
Because it belongs to no single ethnic group, it functions as the neutral language of public life in a country with many local languages.
exampleEn: A radio presenter in Bangui reads the news in French, explains it in Sango, and takes callers who speak either.
qualificationEn: Sango's official status has not displaced French in administration, and its written standard is only loosely observed in everyday use.

expression.glossEn: Hello — a greeting that opens conversations across the Central African Republic

titleEn: Yoruba greetings that name the hour, the age and the standing
facts: Yoruba has different greetings for morning (Ẹ kú àárọ̀), afternoon (Ẹ kú ọ̀sán) and evening (Ẹ kú ìrọ̀lẹ́), so a greeting immediately states when the meeting happens.
The prefix Ẹ is an honorific form used for elders and strangers; dropping it can claim intimacy or signal a lapse in respect.
Younger men traditionally prostrate (dọ̀bálẹ̀) and younger women kneel (kúnlẹ̀) when greeting elders in many Yoruba families, though urban and diaspora practice varies.
Yoruba is tonal: the same syllable at a different pitch can be a different word, so greetings must be voiced with the right tones to be understood.
Greeting is an obligation rather than small talk; going straight to business without it can read as rudeness, especially with older people.
exampleEn: A young man enters a family compound in Ibadan, greets each elder in turn and prostrates briefly before explaining why he has come.
qualificationEn: Practice is not uniform: many Lagos and diaspora families have dropped kneeling and prostration, and Christian and Muslim households use different greeting formulas.

expression.glossEn: Good morning — the honorific Ẹ marks respect for the person greeted

region: West Africa — Yoruba and Ewe areas
titleEn: When the drum is the sentence: speech surrogacy in West Africa
facts: The hourglass-shaped talking drum, held under the arm and squeezed to change pitch, can imitate the tones and rhythm of Yoruba, Ewe and other tonal languages.
Yoruba dùndún players use set phrases and oríkì (praise names) to 'say' greetings, proverbs and genealogies at ceremonies.
The drum is not a code for every message: it works best where tone carries meaning, so it conveys formulaic speech far more reliably than arbitrary sentences.
In the 20th century drums announced news and summoned people; today they mostly appear at weddings, naming ceremonies and festivals alongside amplified music.
Church and mosque life reshaped the practice: some Christian communities banned drumming, others adopted it, and oríkì-style praise fed into hymn and gospel forms.
exampleEn: At a Lagos wedding the dùndún player praises the bride's family by name, and the guests respond to phrases they recognise without being told what was said.
qualificationEn: Speech surrogacy is partial and conventional; not every drum phrase is understood by every listener, and Ewe and Yoruba drum traditions differ substantially.

expression.glossEn: the hourglass 'talking' drum, whose tension cords are squeezed to imitate speech tones

titleEn: The shebeen: drinking, licences and sociability after apartheid
facts: Shebeens were unlicensed bars that sold alcohol in South African townships when apartheid law restricted Black people from buying and drinking in licensed venues.
They became social institutions — a back room, a fridge, a radio and a host who knew everyone, often run by women.
After 1994 many shebeens obtained licences while others stayed informal, and the word travelled to Namibia, Zimbabwe, Zambia and Malawi.
Today they are places for conversation, music and local news, sitting alongside taverns and bottle stores in the township economy.
Researchers also record the risks: alcohol harm, policing and competition with the formal liquor trade are recurring local debates.
exampleEn: On a Friday evening in a Free State township, neighbours gather in a converted garage, share a crate of beer and catch up on funerals, jobs and football.
qualificationEn: Shebeens are not uniform — Cape Town, Durban and Windhoek variants differ in legality, clientele and music — and the word can carry a stigma.

titleEn: Boda boda: the motorcycle taxis that keep Ugandan cities moving
facts: Boda boda are bicycle or motorcycle taxis common across East Africa, and the term itself is Ugandan and Kenyan; in Kenya they are also called piki piki.
They fill gaps left by buses and matatus, reaching unpaved neighbourhoods and carrying passengers, sacks, chickens and furniture.
Riders usually belong to stage-based associations that set routes, prices and dispute rules, and the stages double as social hubs.
Regulation is contested: helmets, licences, night curfews and safety campaigns recur, and Kampala has repeatedly tried to restrict riders from the city centre.
The work is a major youth employer and a source of quick cash, though earnings are volatile and road crashes are a public-health concern.
exampleEn: A trader in Kampala pays a rider to carry two sacks of maize to her stall because no taxi will take the load.
qualificationEn: Rules and practices differ by city and stage; Kampala's restrictions, Nairobi's piki piki culture and rural services are not interchangeable.

titleEn: The kanga: a cloth that speaks in proverbs
facts: A kanga is a printed cotton wrap about 1.5 by 1 metre, worn in the African Great Lakes region and normally sold in pairs.
Each cloth has a border, a central field (mji) and often a Swahili proverb or message printed along the edge.
The message can congratulate, tease, warn or mourn, so the kanga is chosen for what it says as much as for its pattern.
Kangas serve as skirts, dresses, head coverings and baby slings, and they are given at weddings, births and funerals.
Factory-printed designs track politics, football and fashion, and the cloth is a cheap, visible way to make a public statement.
exampleEn: A mother-in-law gives her new daughter-in-law a kanga printed with a proverb about patience, and the message is read aloud at the ceremony.
qualificationEn: Kanga messages are not always serious and their meaning depends on context; Tanzanian and Kenyan printing traditions differ, and kitenge is a heavier, related cloth.

titleEn: Thirteen months and a seven-year gap: the Ethiopian calendar
facts: Ethiopia uses its own calendar, derived from the Coptic and Ge'ez tradition, with twelve months of 30 days and a thirteenth month of five or six days.
The Ethiopian year runs about seven to eight years behind the Gregorian year, so dates on Ethiopian documents must be converted.
New Year (Enkutatash) falls on 11 September, or 12 September in a leap year, just as the rains end.
Time is also counted differently in everyday speech: the Ethiopian clock starts at dawn, so a stated '7 o'clock' can mean 1 a.m. in international time.
Schools, churches, government offices and newspapers use Ethiopian dates alongside Gregorian ones, and the calendar is a marker of national identity.
exampleEn: A hotel in Addis Ababa prints a meeting time in both calendars so guests do not miss a date that lies seven years apart between systems.
qualificationEn: The calendar is official in Ethiopia but is not Eritrea's civil calendar today, and conversion depends on the leap-year cycle, so dates should be checked rather than estimated.

titleEn: Akan day names: the weekday that becomes a person
facts: Akan families in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire name children after the day of the week they were born, and these day names carry meanings about character and soul.
Examples include Kwame (Saturday-born male), Ama (Saturday-born female), Kofi (Friday) and Akosua (Sunday).
Middle names are more varied and can mark birth order, twin status or an ancestor, and Christian or Muslim names are often added alongside.
Day names are used in daily address, school registers and official documents, so one person may be known by different names in different settings.
The practice has travelled with the African diaspora, and Ghanaian families abroad still give day names.
exampleEn: A student in Accra is called Kwame by his grandmother, Michael on his passport, and K. by his football coach, and all three names are correct.
qualificationEn: Naming practice varies among Akan subgroups and between Christian and Muslim families, and not every Ghanaian is Akan or uses day names.

titleEn: The 1929 Women's War: when Igbo women policed colonial power
facts: In November 1929 thousands of Igbo women marched on Oloko and other towns to protest the warrant chiefs appointed by the British and the taxes they imposed.
The women used 'sitting on a man' — a traditional sanction of public shaming, song and disruption — against officials and chiefs.
The unrest spread across Aba, Owerri and Calabar provinces, and colonial police killed more than 50 women during the repression that followed.
The protests forced the British to reconsider the warrant-chief system, and the event is remembered as an early anti-colonial movement led by women.
It shows how gendered institutions worked: women's councils and market networks were political structures, not only domestic ones.
exampleEn: Women from several villages travel together, sing mocking songs outside a warrant chief's compound, and refuse to leave until he answers them.
qualificationEn: The Women's War was not a single organisation or a nationalist party; its aims and participants varied locally, and its history has been interpreted differently since.

titleEn: Xeer: Somali customary law and the elders who negotiate it
facts: Xeer is the customary legal system used by Somali communities in Somalia, Djibouti, the Somali Region of Ethiopia and north-eastern Kenya.
It works through elders and clan representatives who negotiate compensation, marriage and resource disputes according to precedent.
Xeer predates Islam in the region but has absorbed Islamic principles, and it coexists with civil and sharia courts.
Its strength is negotiation and restitution rather than punishment, which can stop disputes escalating between groups.
Its weakness is that it depends on clan membership, so women, minorities and people outside clan networks can be disadvantaged.
exampleEn: After a road accident, elders from two clans meet, hear witnesses, and agree on diya (compensation) paid in livestock or cash.
qualificationEn: Xeer is not codified and varies by region and clan; it has been praised for local legitimacy and criticised for excluding weaker parties.

titleEn: Touba and the Mouride order: faith, work and a city built by disciples
facts: The Mouride order is a Sufi brotherhood founded in Senegal by Sheikh Amadou Bamba (1853–1927) and headquartered in Touba.
It is known for the doctrine of work as worship: disciples combine religious devotion with farming, trading and urban labour.
Touba, now a city of more than a million people, grew around Bamba's tomb and the Grand Mosque, and it is administered largely by the order rather than the state.
The annual Grand Magal pilgrimage brings millions of Mourides to Touba and is a major social and economic event.
Mouride networks link Senegal to migrant communities in Europe and North America, and their trading networks are studied as a form of religious economy.
exampleEn: A Mouride trader in Dakar closes his shop for the Magal, travels to Touba, and comes back with blessings and new business contacts.
qualificationEn: Senegal's Sufi landscape includes the Tijaniyya and other orders, and Mouride practice differs between rural disciples and urban merchants.

titleEn: The annual replastering of Djenné's great mosque
facts: The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali is the largest adobe building in the world, and the present structure dates from 1907, replacing an earlier mosque on the site.
Each year before the rainy season, residents and visitors gather to replaster the walls in a communal working party known as the crépissage, using mud mixed with rice husks and water.
The work is organised by masons' guilds and neighbourhood groups, and it renews both the building and the town's social ties.
The mosque sits at the centre of Djenné's market and festival life, and the town's old quarter is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Conservation debates pit local maintenance traditions against heritage rules that restrict changes to the building.
exampleEn: Young men carry baskets of mud up scaffolding of palm branches while women and children hand up water, and the whole town works to a rhythm of drumming.
qualificationEn: The replastering is a local tradition with variations, and the mosque's management involves religious authorities, the state and heritage bodies, so simple descriptions can mislead.

titleEn: Gacaca: Rwanda's grass-roots courts after the genocide
facts: Gacaca courts were Rwanda's community-based justice system, revived in 2001 to try people accused of crimes during the 1994 genocide.
The name means 'short grass' and refers to the open meeting place where village elders traditionally resolved disputes.
Elected lay judges heard testimony in public, aiming at confession, truth-telling and reintegration rather than courtroom procedure.
Around 12,000 gacaca courts processed more than a million cases between 2002 and 2012.
Supporters credit it with clearing a vast backlog and enabling local reconciliation; critics point to weak legal safeguards, intimidation and limited appeal.
exampleEn: In a village courtyard, survivors and neighbours sit on benches while elected judges hear a man describe what happened to a family in 1994.
qualificationEn: Gacaca was a transitional mechanism with explicit political aims; evaluations differ sharply, and it should not be described as a model that can be copied uncritically.

titleEn: Kuomboka: the Lozi king's journey out of the flood
facts: Kuomboka means 'to get out of water' in Lozi, and it marks the end of the rainy season when the upper Zambezi floods the Barotse plain.
The Litunga, king of the Lozi, travels by royal barge from Lealui to Limulunga, accompanied by drumming, singing and paddlers in ceremonial dress.
The main barge, the Nalikwanda, is painted black and white like a zebra, and crowds gather on the higher ground to watch it pass.
The ceremony is both a practical response to the annual flood and a performance of Lozi kingship and identity.
Zambia recognises it as a national ceremony, and it draws visitors and researchers interested in Lozi history and floodplain management.
exampleEn: Drummers begin days before the crossing, and families along the route camp on high ground to watch the barge pass.
qualificationEn: The ceremony's date follows the flood rather than a fixed calendar date, and Lozi politics and royal succession have shaped how it is performed over time.

titleEn: Abusua: Akan identity through the mother's line
facts: Abusua is the Akan term for a matrilineal group descended from a common ancestress, and a person belongs to the mother's abusua for life.
Inheritance of property, political office and certain ritual roles traditionally follows the abusua line, even where fathers provide for their children.
Each abusua is associated with particular abosom (deities) and taboos, and members share obligations at funerals and naming ceremonies.
There are seven ancient abusua in Akan tradition, with many more subgroups, and the system organises both kinship and local politics.
The mother's brother (wɔfa) has a recognised role in a child's upbringing and in settling disputes, and Akan chiefs are chosen through abusua lines.
exampleEn: At an Akan funeral, the mourning and the distribution of property are led by the deceased's abusua rather than by the widower's family.
qualificationEn: Practice varies between Asante, Fante and other Akan groups, and urban migration, Christianity and formal law have changed how inheritance is handled.

titleEn: Lobolo: marriage as a negotiation between families
facts: Lobolo (lobola) is the transfer of livestock or goods from a groom's family to a bride's family, practised among Zulu, Xhosa, Swazi, Ndebele and other southern African societies.
It is not a purchase of a wife: the negotiations recognise the bride's family's loss and create lasting obligations and ties between two families.
Amounts and forms vary widely; cattle are traditional in many areas, while urban families increasingly agree on cash, instalments or a symbolic number of animals.
Elders and go-betweens conduct the negotiations, which can take months, and a couple may live together before lobolo is completed.
The cost of lobolo for young men, and its relationship to gender equality, are recurring subjects in South African public debate.
exampleEn: Two families meet at the bride's home, exchange greetings, and begin the formal request for lobolo, with the bride's uncle speaking for her family.
qualificationEn: Lobolo is not one practice — Zulu, Xhosa, Swazi and Tsonga customs differ — and civil or church marriage is often combined with it in different ways.

titleEn: Kwanjula: the Baganda introduction that makes a marriage
facts: Kwanjula is the Baganda introduction ceremony in which a groom and his family are formally presented to the bride's family.
It is the customary marriage contract in Kiganda culture, involving gift-giving, speeches and the public naming of the relationship.
The bride's family hosts and can accept or question the groom, and the event is usually large, with food, music and emcees.
The gomesi, a floor-length dress, is the usual attire for women at kwanjula, while men wear the kanzu.
Urban Ugandans often hold kwanjula alongside church or civil weddings, and the event has become a major expense and social display.
exampleEn: A groom's delegation arrives with baskets of fruit and envelopes, is greeted by the bride's aunties, and waits while the family discusses the request.
qualificationEn: Kwanjula is specific to Buganda; other Ugandan societies have different introduction customs, and Christian denominations vary in how they treat it.

titleEn: Cattle as kinship: Dinka life in South Sudan
facts: The Dinka are a Nilotic people of South Sudan whose livelihood and social life centre on cattle kept along the Nile and its floodplains.
Cattle are used for bridewealth, funerals, compensation and naming, and a family's standing is often described through its herd.
Young men take named oxen, compose songs about them and decorate their horns; cattle camps move with the seasons between river and grazing land.
Milk and sorghum are staples, supplemented by fish and wild foods, and cattle also provide hides and dung for floors and fires.
Decades of war, displacement and climate stress have disrupted herds, and many Dinka now live in towns or abroad while maintaining cattle ties.
exampleEn: A young man in a cattle camp sings a song about his favourite ox, and the song becomes a way of courting and of recording family history.
qualificationEn: Dinka society is not homogeneous — there are many sections and clans — and Nuer and other Nilotic neighbours have related but distinct cattle traditions.

titleEn: Jollof rice and the politics of the shared pot
facts: Jollof rice is a one-pot dish of rice cooked with tomatoes, peppers, onions and spices, claimed by Senegal, The Gambia, Ghana, Nigeria and other West African countries.
The name is usually traced to the Wolof people of Senegambia, and the Senegalese rice dish thieboudienne is an older relative.
Cooking is social: the pot is large, the rice steams over a low fire, and the layer at the bottom (the 'party rice' crust) is prized.
The Ghana–Nigeria 'jollof wars' are a running public joke and a genuine point of pride, staged on social media and at festivals.
Jollof is standard at weddings, funerals and political rallies, and the quality of the pot is a public measure of hospitality.
exampleEn: At a Lagos wedding, two aunties argue about whether the jollof should be smoky, and the caterer is judged on the crust at the bottom of the pot.
qualificationEn: Recipes differ by country and household, and the dish should not be treated as one national possession; Senegalese, Ghanaian and Nigerian versions are genuinely different.

titleEn: The Ethiopian coffee ceremony: three rounds and a social order
facts: The coffee ceremony (buna) is a daily social ritual in Ethiopia and Eritrea, usually hosted by a woman who roasts green beans over charcoal.
The host roasts, grinds and brews the coffee in a jebena clay pot and serves three rounds: abol, tona and bereka.
Guests are served in order of age and status, and incense plus popcorn or bread accompany the coffee.
Declining coffee politely usually means tea will be offered instead, and the ceremony is a way to receive neighbours and exchange news.
The ritual takes an hour or more, and it belongs to hospitality, mourning and celebration rather than to a quick caffeine break.
exampleEn: A neighbour arrives unannounced in Addis Ababa; the host lights charcoal, roasts beans, and the visit becomes an afternoon of conversation over three cups.
qualificationEn: Practice varies between Orthodox Christian, Muslim and urban households, and city cafés often serve coffee quickly rather than performing the full ceremony.

sources.title: Coffee ceremony of Ethiopia and Eritrea

titleEn: FESPACO: Ouagadougou's biennial argument about African cinema
facts: FESPACO is the Panafrican Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou, held in Burkina Faso's capital in odd-numbered years.
It accepts for competition only films by African filmmakers, chiefly produced in Africa, and its top prize is the Étalon d'or de Yennenga.
The festival began in 1969 and became a meeting point for directors, critics and audiences from across the continent.
Its opening night is held at the Stade du 4-Août, and screenings spread across the city's cinemas.
FESPACO has shaped debates about funding, distribution and language in African film, and it is a major cultural event for Burkina Faso.
exampleEn: A young Burkinabè director saves for a year to attend FESPACO, queues for a screening and pitches a script in a hotel lobby.
qualificationEn: The festival's scale and influence have fluctuated with Burkina Faso's security situation and funding, and its biennial rhythm has changed at times.

sources.title: Panafrican Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou

titleEn: Susu: saving together when banks are far away
facts: Susu (also sou-sou, osusu or asue) is a rotating savings and credit association used in West Africa and the Caribbean.
Members contribute the same amount at fixed intervals, and each period one member receives the whole pot; the order is agreed in advance.
In Ghana and Sierra Leone, susu collectors may hold the money for a fee and keep records, acting as informal bankers.
The system depends on trust and social pressure rather than collateral or contracts, and it works where formal banking is expensive or distant.
It funds school fees, market stock, funerals and small businesses, and it has adapted to mobile money in recent years.
exampleEn: Ten market women in Kumasi each pay 100 cedis a week, and one of them takes the 1,000-cedi pot each week in a rota agreed at the start.
qualificationEn: Susu arrangements vary by country and collector; they are not regulated like banks, and disputes depend on community sanctions rather than courts.

titleEn: Stokvels: South Africa's savings clubs as social insurance
facts: A stokvel is an invitation-only South African savings club, typically of twelve or more members who contribute fixed sums weekly, fortnightly or monthly.
The name comes from 'stock fairs', the rotating cattle auctions held by English settlers in the Eastern Cape in the early 19th century.
Members take turns receiving the pooled money, and many stokvels also run burial funds, grocery schemes and investment accounts.
Stokvels are a major part of Black South African financial life, and estimates of the money they hold run into the tens of billions of rand.
They are governed by written or spoken rules and social accountability, and disputes are handled at meetings rather than in court.
exampleEn: A group of nurses in Soweto runs a stokvel that pays out in December for school clothes and groceries, with a separate burial fund.
qualificationEn: Stokvels differ widely in size, purpose and formality, and some have been vehicles for pyramid schemes or fraud, so the sector is not uniformly safe.

titleEn: M-Pesa: how a phone became the bank branch
facts: M-Pesa launched in Kenya in 2007 as a mobile money service run by Safaricom and Vodafone, originally to collect microfinance repayments.
Users deposit and withdraw cash through small shop agents and send money by phone; the service later expanded to Tanzania, Mozambique, DR Congo, Lesotho, Ghana, Egypt and Ethiopia.
It changed how people pay for matatu rides, school fees, vegetables and remittances, especially where bank branches are scarce.
The network of agents became a new layer of local commerce, and M-Pesa receipts are accepted as proof of payment.
Regulators and banks had to adapt, and mobile money raised questions about fees, data and the exclusion of people without phones.
exampleEn: A matatu conductor in Nairobi sends change through M-Pesa because neither he nor the passenger has small notes.
qualificationEn: M-Pesa's success is specific to Kenya's market and regulation; Tanzania's M-Pesa and mobile money in Ghana and elsewhere have different histories and fee structures.

titleEn: Makola Market: women traders and the making of Accra's centre
facts: Makola Market sits in central Accra and is one of West Africa's largest open-air trading complexes.
It is dominated by women traders selling produce, cloth, household goods, medicines and imported items, and the market is a major employer.
Trade runs on networks and credit relationships, and 'market queens' who lead commodity associations can influence prices and politics.
The market's location and history are tied to Accra's growth and to colonial attempts to regulate and relocate traders.
In 1979, and at other times, military governments cleared or demolished parts of the market, and traders rebuilt around the disruption.
exampleEn: A trader at Makola extends credit to a customer she has known for years, noting the debt in a notebook rather than in a bank system.
qualificationEn: Makola is not one market but a district of stalls and streets, and the 'market queen' system is documented unevenly and differs by commodity.

titleEn: Matatu: Nairobi's privately run public transport
facts: Matatus are privately owned minibuses that carry most commuter trips in Nairobi and other Kenyan cities — over 70 percent in Nairobi by some estimates.
They are often decorated with portraits of musicians and politicians, slogans, lights and sound systems, and the decoration is part of a vehicle's appeal.
Routes, stages and fares are managed by savings and credit groups and stage associations that negotiate with the county government.
Matatu culture has produced slang, fashion and music, and it is a space where young people work as drivers, conductors and touts.
Crashes, congestion and informal fees are persistent problems, and the 2004 Michuki rules introduced seat belts and speed limits.
exampleEn: A conductor hangs out of the door shouting the destination while the driver plays a track chosen to pull passengers from the rival bus behind.
qualificationEn: Regulation and style vary between Nairobi, Mombasa and smaller towns, and conditions are often poorer than the decorated exterior suggests.

titleEn: Umuganda: Rwanda's monthly communal work
facts: Umuganda takes place on the last Saturday of every month from 08:00 to 11:00 and is a mandatory nationwide community service.
Residents clean roads, build houses for vulnerable people, plant trees and repair infrastructure, then hold a community meeting.
Participation is required by law, and failure to take part can be fined; the policy is presented as a revival of a pre-colonial tradition of mutual aid.
The meeting after the work is used for announcements, dispute resolution and government messaging.
Critics note that mandatory service and the meeting format also work as social control, while supporters point to visible improvements and local participation.
exampleEn: On a Saturday morning in Kigali, neighbours clear a drainage channel together, then sit under a tree to hear local officials and raise complaints.
qualificationEn: Umuganda's origins and meanings are debated, and its compulsory character distinguishes it from voluntary community work elsewhere in the region.

titleEn: Kgotla: Botswana's public assembly and the rule of consensus
facts: A kgotla is a public meeting, community council and traditional court in Botswana, and similar institutions exist in rural Lesotho and South Africa.
It is headed by a chief or headman who works with advisers, and community decisions are reached by consensus after everyone has spoken.
Speaking is ordered: no one may interrupt while another is having their say, and the assembly is the accepted place to raise grievances.
Botswana's reputation for stable democracy is often linked to kgotla traditions of public deliberation, though the institution is also shaped by party politics.
The kgotla is used for land allocation, dispute settlement and consultation on policy, and urban residents often return to their home villages for it.
exampleEn: A land dispute in a Botswana village goes to the kgotla, where both families speak in turn before the chief announces a decision the community accepts.
qualificationEn: Kgotla practice varies across Botswana's ethnic groups and has been criticised for keeping young people and women out of speaking positions.

titleEn: Highlife: the dance-band music of West Africa's ports
facts: Highlife developed in the coastal cities of present-day Ghana in the 19th century, blending local rhythms with Western instruments and jazz melodies.
Its name is often linked to the expensive 'high life' of colonial elites and to the dance halls where the music was played.
The style is marked by jazzy horns, guitars and the two-finger plucking technique borrowed from palm-wine music.
As it travelled to Nigeria, highlife became bigger and more orchestral, and it fed into the later development of Afrobeat.
After independence it remained social music for weddings, funerals and political rallies, and younger artists have revived it.
exampleEn: At a Ghanaian funeral, a highlife band plays the deceased's favourite song while mourners dance and donors are announced.
qualificationEn: Highlife is a family of styles rather than one sound; Ghanaian and Nigerian highlife differ, and palm-wine music is a related but distinct tradition.

titleEn: Mbalax: sabar drums at the centre of Senegambian dance music
facts: Mbalax is the urban dance music of Senegal, The Gambia and Mauritania, and its name comes from a Wolof drum rhythm.
It is built on sabar drumming, played by griots and drummers at family ceremonies, and it uses Wolof and French lyrics.
Youssou N'Dour helped develop and globalise the style in the 1970s and 1980s, drawing on Serer njuup and ndut initiation music.
Mbalax songs comment on social issues, praise patrons and tell stories, and dance is a central part of the performance.
Senegalese weddings and naming ceremonies still rely on sabar ensembles before the amplified band takes over.
exampleEn: At a Dakar wedding the sabar players change rhythm and the dancers follow, then a mbalax band starts and the party moves into the courtyard.
qualificationEn: Mbalax is not identical across Senegal and The Gambia, and its modern form has been shaped by recording studios and diaspora audiences.

titleEn: Congolese rumba: two capitals, one guitar line
facts: Congolese rumba developed in Kinshasa and Brazzaville from the 1930s and 1940s, drawing on Cuban son, local rhythms and Lingala lyrics.
It is built on interlocking guitars, a driving bass and vocal harmonies, and it became the dominant dance music of Central Africa.
In December 2021 UNESCO added Congolese rumba to its list of intangible cultural heritage.
Soukous, a faster offshoot with more guitar improvisation, spread to Paris and the wider African diaspora from the 1960s.
Rumba songs are social chronicles, praising patrons, commenting on love and politics, and marking funerals and weddings.
exampleEn: At a Kinshasa wedding the band plays an old rumba standard and three generations sing the Lingala chorus from memory.
qualificationEn: Congolese rumba and soukous are related but distinct, and Congolese and diaspora scenes have diverged since the 1990s.

titleEn: Taarab: Swahili poetry sung with an orchestra
facts: Taarab is a music genre popular in Tanzania and Kenya, closely tied to Zanzibar and the Swahili coast.
It blends African Great Lakes traditions with North African, Middle Eastern and Indian influences, using orchestral instruments and sung Swahili poetry.
Taarab rose to prominence in 1928 with Siti binti Saad, one of the first East African women to record commercially.
Weddings and festivals are its main settings, and songs often praise or criticise individuals and comment on social life.
Modern taarab uses keyboards and drum machines, and it has influenced bongo flava and Swahili pop.
exampleEn: At a Zanzibar wedding a taarab singer performs a song composed for the couple, and the guests listen closely to the lyrics for praise or teasing.
qualificationEn: Taarab has several styles and regional variants, and contemporary Zanzibar taarab differs from older recordings and from Kenyan taarab.

titleEn: Amapiano: log drums and the township dance floor
facts: Amapiano is a South African genre that became popular in the early 2020s, emerging from Johannesburg and Pretoria townships.
It combines kwaito, deep house, gqom, jazz, soul and lounge influences, with distinctive log-drum bass lines and airy synths.
The name comes from the isiZulu word for pianos, and the music spreads through WhatsApp, YouTube and dance challenges.
Its dance culture is social and competitive, and amapiano parties are often all-day events with dancing in circles.
By the 2020s it had become one of Africa's biggest musical exports, with collaborations across the continent and in Europe.
exampleEn: A group of friends in Soweto clear a space in a yard, play amapiano from a speaker, and take turns dancing in the middle of the circle.
qualificationEn: Amapiano is a fast-moving scene with many sub-styles, and its South African origins are often blurred in international coverage.

titleEn: Kizomba: slow dance from Angola's parties
facts: Kizomba is a social dance and music genre that emerged in Angola in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
The word means 'party' in Kimbundu, and the dance developed in family and neighbourhood celebrations before moving into clubs.
Its music blends Angolan semba with zouk and other Caribbean influences, and the dance is close, slow and partner-based.
Kizomba spread to Portugal, France, Cape Verde and Brazil through Angolan and Cape Verdean migration and became a global social-dance scene.
The dance has been criticised for sexualised marketing abroad, while Angolan practitioners emphasise its family and community origins.
exampleEn: At a Luanda family party, older couples dance kizomba to live music while younger relatives film the steps and copy them.
qualificationEn: Kizomba, semba and zouk are often confused; the Angolan form has regional variants, and the international dance scene has changed the style considerably.

titleEn: Laamb: wrestling as village reputation and national sport
facts: Senegalese wrestling (laamb) is a folk wrestling tradition performed by the Serer people and now a national sport in Senegal and The Gambia.
It is one of the few West African wrestling traditions that allows hand strikes (frappe).
Matches are large events with drumming, griots praising the wrestlers and crowds betting on the outcome; a single bout can last seconds.
Wrestlers train in stables, village and neighbourhood identity is at stake, and champions become celebrities.
Sponsorship and television have grown the sport's economics, and top wrestlers earn significant purses.
exampleEn: In a Dakar arena, griots sing a wrestler's praises, the crowd shouts slogans, and a single throw ends the match and settles village bragging rights.
qualificationEn: Senegalese wrestling is distinct from other West African wrestling styles, and its commercial success has changed the traditional village format.

titleEn: Oware: the board game that counts and captures
facts: Oware is a mancala-family strategy game played on a board of pits with seeds, and it is widely believed to be of Ashanti origin.
Two players sow seeds around the board and capture the opponent's seeds by landing in particular positions.
It is played in homes, markets and schools, and skilled players calculate several moves ahead while a crowd watches.
The game is used to teach counting and strategy, and it appears in Ghanaian and Caribbean cultural life.
Boards range from carved wooden pieces to holes dug in the ground, and the rules vary locally.
exampleEn: Two men in a Kumasi market play oware on a carved board while a third watches and points out a missed capture.
qualificationEn: Oware rules vary between regions and households, and mancala games are played across Africa and Asia, so the Ashanti origin is a tradition rather than a settled fact.

titleEn: Nollywood: video storytelling as a national argument
facts: Nollywood is the Nigerian film industry, named by a portmanteau of 'Nigeria' and 'Hollywood' in the early 2000s.
It grew from the 1990s video boom: cheap camcorders, straight-to-video releases and market distribution made films affordable across Africa.
Nigerian films and series tell moral, family, religious and political stories, and they are central to public arguments about wealth, corruption and gender.
The industry employs actors, marketers and technicians and has regional centres, including Hausa-language Kannywood in Kano.
Streaming services and cinemas have changed distribution since the 2010s, while the older video market persists.
exampleEn: A family in Enugu gathers in the evening to watch a new Nollywood release, then argues about whether the ending was moral or merely convenient.
qualificationEn: Nollywood is a loose label for many industries and genres, and the term's meaning has been contested since it was coined.

titleEn: Griots: history, praise and diplomacy in Mandé society
facts: Griots (jeliw in Manding) are West African historians, storytellers, praise singers and musicians, and the role is hereditary in Mandé societies.
They keep genealogies, mediate disputes and perform at weddings, naming ceremonies and political events, often accompanying themselves on the kora.
The Epic of Sundiata, which tells of the founding of the Mali Empire, is griot repertoire performed across generations.
Griots speak with licence: they can praise and criticise patrons, and their words carry social weight.
Their status is complex — respected as keepers of memory but sometimes treated as a separate caste — and the role has adapted to radio, recordings and diaspora.
exampleEn: At a Bamako wedding, a jeli praises the bride's lineage by name and recounts an ancestor's deeds, and the family gives gifts in recognition.
qualificationEn: Griot traditions differ across Mandé, Wolof and other societies, and the word covers a range of roles that are not interchangeable.

titleEn: Izibongo: Zulu praise poetry that can also criticise
facts: Izibongo is a genre of oral poetry among Bantu peoples of southern Africa, especially the Zulu and Xhosa.
It is often called praise poetry, but researchers note that it can contain criticism, warning and satire as well as praise.
Izibongo are performed at weddings, funerals and political gatherings, and they record family histories and public reputations.
Praise poets (imbongi) can address chiefs and politicians in ways ordinary people cannot, and the form has been used in anti-apartheid and contemporary politics.
Written collections and school syllabuses have turned izibongo into a literary genre as well as a performance.
exampleEn: At a rally in KwaZulu-Natal, an imbongi praises the leader's ancestors, then slips in a warning about the community's unmet needs.
qualificationEn: Izibongo vary by language and region, and the translation 'praise poetry' has been criticised for flattening the genre's critical edge.

titleEn: Kente: cloth, status and the politics of wearing
facts: Kente is a Ghanaian hand-woven cloth of silk and cotton strips, and it is officially recognised as a geographical indication of Ghana.
According to Asante oral tradition it originated at Bonwire in the Ashanti Region.
Historically it was worn in toga-like fashion by Asante, Akan and Ewe people, with patterns carrying names and meanings.
Today kente is worn at graduations, weddings, funerals and church services, and by Ghanaians abroad as a marker of identity.
Its commercialisation has raised debates about authenticity, machine-printed imitations and who may wear particular patterns.
exampleEn: A Ghanaian graduate in Accra wears a kente stole over a gown, and the pattern's name is announced while family members take photographs.
qualificationEn: Kente designs and meanings vary between Asante and Ewe weaving traditions, and much 'kente-print' fabric on the market is not hand-woven.

titleEn: La Sape: dressing well as a moral position
facts: La Sape is a fashion subculture centred on Kinshasa and Brazzaville, and its name derives from the Société des Ambianceurs et des Personnes Élégantes.
Adherents, called sapeurs, wear expensive designer clothes and cultivate elegance, manners and public performance.
The movement has roots in colonial-era servants who adopted European dress, and it later became a statement of dignity amid economic crisis.
Sapeurs often spend large sums on clothes relative to their income, and the practice has been read as both conspicuous consumption and self-respect.
La Sape has influenced Congolese music videos and fashion photography, and sapeurs appear in European cities with Congolese communities.
exampleEn: On a Sunday in Bacongo, a sapeur walks to church in a tailored suit and polished shoes, greeting friends who admire the colour combination.
qualificationEn: La Sape is not a single organisation, and its practices differ between Kinshasa, Brazzaville and diaspora scenes; not all Congolese see it as admirable.

titleEn: The capulana: Mozambique's everyday cloth
facts: A capulana is a sarong-like length of cloth about 2 by 1 metres, worn primarily in Mozambique and south-eastern Africa.
It can be a skirt, a dress, a headwrap, a baby carrier or a carried bundle, and it is treated as a complete piece of clothing.
Capulanas are printed in bright patterns, and particular designs mark weddings, mourning and everyday wear.
They are sold in markets and given as gifts, and the cloth is used in ceremonies and as a marker of respect.
The capulana has entered contemporary Mozambican fashion and art, and it is also used in political and religious contexts.
exampleEn: At a Maputo market a woman chooses a capulana with a pattern suitable for a funeral, then buys a brighter one for her daughter's wedding.
qualificationEn: Pattern conventions differ by region and family, and similar cloths under other names are worn across southern Africa.

titleEn: Transhumance: moving with the rains in the Sahel
facts: Transhumance is the seasonal movement of livestock between fixed pastures, practised by Fulani and other pastoralists across the Sahel.
Herds move north during the rainy season and south in the dry season, following grass and water and crossing national borders.
Routes are established by custom and negotiated with farming communities, but they are increasingly blocked by fields, roads and climate stress.
Conflicts between herders and farmers over crop damage and water access have become more frequent and politically charged.
Pastoralist economies supply meat, milk and animal traction, and transhumance is a form of land use adapted to unpredictable rainfall.
exampleEn: In the dry season a Fulani family drives cattle south past harvested fields, paying a negotiated fee to cross farmland and reach a water point.
qualificationEn: Transhumance is often confused with nomadic pastoralism; routes and arrangements differ between countries, and not all Fulani are pastoralists.

titleEn: Ifá: divination as a system of knowledge
facts: Ifá is a Yoruba geomantic divination system in which a diviner (babalawo) casts palm nuts or a chain to produce one of 256 signs.
Each sign has associated verses (ese Ifá) that encode mythology, history, medicine and ethics, and the diviner interprets them for the client.
Ifá is consulted about marriage, illness, business and travel, and it is also a religious practice linked to Orisha worship.
The system is learned through long apprenticeship and memorisation, and it has been carried to Cuba, Brazil and the United States.
UNESCO recognised Ifá divination as intangible cultural heritage in 2005.
exampleEn: A family in Oyo consults a babalawo before a marriage, and the verses he recites are discussed as guidance rather than a fixed prediction.
qualificationEn: Ifá practice varies between Nigeria, Benin and the diaspora, and its verses are interpreted rather than applied mechanically.

titleEn: Vodún: lived religion in Benin and Togo
facts: Vodún is a traditional religion practised by Aja, Ewe and Fon peoples in Benin, Togo, Ghana and Nigeria, with no central authority.
It centres on vodún (spirits or deities) associated with natural forces, ancestors and particular places, served through priests and shrines.
Practitioners make offerings, consult diviners and hold ceremonies with drumming and dance, and the religion is embedded in family and community life.
Benin's government has promoted Vodún as national heritage, and Ouidah hosts an annual Vodún festival.
Vodún travelled to the Americas with enslaved Africans and shaped Haitian Vodou, Cuban Santería and Brazilian Candomblé.
exampleEn: In Ouidah a family honours its vodún at a shrine with offerings, drumming and shared food, and neighbours join the ceremony.
qualificationEn: Vodún is often sensationalised in foreign media; it is a diverse lived religion, and its relationship to diaspora religions is historical rather than identical.

titleEn: Bwiti: initiation and ancestor knowledge in Gabon
facts: Bwiti is a spiritual discipline of the Punu and Mitsogo peoples of Gabon, also practised by Fang communities.
It centres on initiation, ancestor veneration and the use of iboga, a plant with psychoactive properties, in controlled ceremonies.
Modern Bwiti combines animism, ancestor worship and, in some cases, Christianity into a syncretic system.
Initiation involves instruction, music and a long ceremony, and it marks entry into adulthood and community responsibility.
Bwiti has spread to other parts of Central Africa and to Europe, and iboga's therapeutic use is now studied and regulated.
exampleEn: An initiate in southern Gabon prepares for a night-long ceremony with drumming, confession and teaching from elders.
qualificationEn: Bwiti has many branches and local variations, and outsiders' descriptions often emphasise iboga while missing the ethical and community teaching.

titleEn: Famadihana: turning the ancestors in Madagascar
facts: Famadihana is a Malagasy funerary tradition in which families bring ancestors' bodies from the tomb, rewrap them in new cloth and rewrite their names.
The ceremony includes music, dancing and shared food, and it is a joyful occasion as well as a solemn one.
It is practised mainly by highland groups such as the Merina and Betsileo, and it honours ancestors and renews family ties.
The ritual has been criticised by some Christian churches and public-health officials, and it declined during plague outbreaks and the COVID-19 pandemic.
It is expensive, and families may postpone it for years while saving the money.
exampleEn: A family in Antananarivo hires a band, gathers relatives from abroad, and carries the rewrapped ancestors around the tomb before returning them.
qualificationEn: Famadihana is not universal in Madagascar; coastal and Muslim communities have different burial practices, and the tradition has changed over time.

region: Transnational — Horn of Africa and diaspora
titleEn: The Somali diaspora and the trust that moves money
facts: The Somali diaspora grew sharply after the civil war of the early 1990s, with communities in Europe, North America, the Middle East and across Africa.
The UN estimated about 2 million Somalis living outside Greater Somalia in 2015, and remittances are a major part of Somalia's economy.
Hawala (xawilaad) is an informal value-transfer system based on trust between brokers: a sender gives money to one broker and a recipient collects it from another.
Money moves by phone and text message, with brokers settling accounts later, which makes it faster and cheaper than formal banks in many areas.
Diaspora money pays for food, school fees and business investment, and it has been both praised for resilience and scrutinised for regulation and fraud risks.
exampleEn: A mother in Minneapolis sends 200 dollars through a Somali-owned hawala agent, and within an hour her cousin collects the cash in Hargeisa.
qualificationEn: Diaspora experiences differ greatly by host country, and hawala is not unique to Somalis, nor is it automatically illegal; regulation varies by state.

titleEn: Cape Malay: a community built from the Indian Ocean
facts: Cape Malays (Cape Muslims) are a South African ethnic group descended from enslaved and free Muslims brought from Indonesia, South Asia and other parts of the Indian Ocean world during Dutch and British rule.
They shaped the Bo-Kaap neighbourhood of Cape Town, where the Nurul Islam Mosque was established in 1844.
The community developed a distinctive cuisine, ghoema music and Afrikaans-Arabic religious texts.
Under apartheid the group was classified as 'Coloured', and forced removals reshaped Cape Muslim neighbourhoods.
The label 'Cape Malay' is contested because the community's origins are diverse and its members speak Afrikaans rather than Malay today.
exampleEn: In Bo-Kaap, families prepare a Cape Malay meal for Eid and neighbours walk between houses to greet and share food.
qualificationEn: Cape Malay identity is not the same as Malay identity in Malaysia or Indonesia, and many Cape Muslims reject the ethnic label.

titleEn: Ghana Must Go: the 1983 expulsions and their memory
facts: In January 1983 Nigeria's President Shehu Shagari ordered undocumented immigrants to leave, and over two million West African migrants were deported, including about one million Ghanaians.
The episode is remembered as 'Ghana Must Go', a phrase that also became the name of the cheap woven bag many migrants carried.
The expulsions followed an oil-price collapse and economic crisis, and migrants were blamed for unemployment and crime.
Ghana and Nigeria later repaired relations, and the two countries continue to share migration and trade.
The episode is a reminder that pan-African solidarity and national immigration policy have often been in tension.
exampleEn: A Ghanaian worker in Lagos packs his belongings into a checkered bag and joins a crowded lorry to the border after hearing the order on the radio.
qualificationEn: Accounts of the numbers vary, and the use of the phrase as a bag name is later popular memory rather than official terminology.

titleEn: Article 15: the Congolese joke that became a survival code
facts: 'Article 15' is a humorous French-language idiom in the Democratic Republic of the Congo describing an imaginary legal provision that permits any measure needed to survive hardship.
The phrase borrows the formal language of constitutional articles, but the provision it names does not exist; the joke is that hardship requires you to invent your own rules.
Kinshasa residents invoke it to justify whatever circumstances demand — informal work, borrowing, rule-bending — and it is usually said with a shrug and a laugh.
The idiom reflects the gap between formal rules and daily practice, and it circulates in music, comedy and political commentary.
A similar phrase is used in neighbouring Congo-Brazzaville to describe getting by through cleverness.
exampleEn: A civil servant asks for a small bribe and calls it Article 15, laughing, while the queue behind him waits.
qualificationEn: The phrase is humorous but it can describe real corruption and informality; it should not be treated as a simple national trait, and its use varies by class and city.

region: Francophone West Africa and the Caribbean
titleEn: Négritude: the Paris debates that reframed Black culture
facts: Négritude was a framework of critique and literary theory developed in the 1930s by francophone intellectuals and writers in Paris.
Its progenitors include Aimé Césaire of Martinique, Léon Damas of French Guiana and Léopold Sédar Senghor of Senegal.
It asserted Black cultural values against colonial assimilation and influenced independence-era politics and literature.
Senghor, Senegal's first president from 1960 to 1980, promoted Négritude as cultural policy and was the driving force behind the first World Festival of Black Arts in Dakar in 1966.
Critics from Wole Soyinka onward have attacked Négritude for defining Blackness through colonial categories.
exampleEn: Students in Dakar read Senghor's poems in school and debate whether Négritude celebrated African culture or invented an exotic version of it.
qualificationEn: Négritude was not a single doctrine, and its francophone, Caribbean and African versions differ; it is as much a subject of critique as a legacy.
